mainTopic: Ending the previous משנה (drilling, 'זה הכלל', the anvil), the משנה on field labors and their minimum amounts, and the משנה on writing two letters
overview: The גמרא finishes the previous משנה. It explains how drilling a tiny hole counts as a finished מלאכה even for שמואל, what the words 'זה הכלל' add, and why striking an anvil makes one liable: the משכן metalworkers did it, not because it trains the hand. A new משנה then teaches that plowing, weeding, and pruning make one liable for any amount, while gathering wood or grass has a minimum that depends on the purpose. A ברייתא gives similar purpose-based measures for cutting plants. The גמרא asks why every cut does not count as improving the land, and answers with a swamp (רבה and רב יוסף) or someone else's field (אביי). Next, a משנה rules that writing two letters makes one liable, with reasons from רבי יוסי (marking, as on the boards of the משכן) and רבי יהודה (a short name inside a longer one). The גמרא explains why the left hand counts: either an ambidextrous person (אביי) or the view of רבי יוסי. Finally, it asks whether רבי יהודה requires two different letters, and begins quoting a ברייתא on 'מאחת' that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה's rule: drilling any size hole makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line from the משנה that one who drills a hole of any size on שבת is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who drills a hole of any size is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the earlier משנה so it can discuss it. This is a setup for the question that comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says even a tiny hole is enough for liability. The גמרא will now test this rule against the earlier argument between רב and שמואל about making holes.

keyTerms.meaning: Any amount at all, even the smallest
Liable (for a קרבן or punishment for breaking שבת)

phrases.english: One who drills any amount — is liable.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה on 102b.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this passage by quoting the משנה line about to be examined.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Drilling a hole of any size on שבת makes one חייב.

steps.title: According to שמואל, drilling is not a finished labor
steps.stepSummary: The rule works for רב, who sees a hole as a kind of building, but שמואל holds that a hole is not a finished job, so why is the driller liable?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense according to רב: the driller looks like someone making a hole as part of building. But according to שמואל, drilling is not the finishing of a labor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה using שמואל's opinion. Drilling a hole should not count as finishing anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier (102b), רב said making a hole falls under בונה, so drilling here fits easily. שמואל said the liability for a hole comes from מכה בפטיש, the final finishing blow. A drilled hole is usually waiting for a peg to be put in, so the job is not done yet. That makes it hard to see why the driller is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (for one view), the opening of a 'this works for X but not for Y' challenge
The completion of a labor (the idea behind מכה בפטיש)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a challenge to רב. The 'בשלמא... אלא' format means: this works for one opinion (רב) but not for the other (שמואל).

phrases.english: It makes sense according to Rav —
he looks like one who makes a hole for building,
but according to Shmuel —
it is not a completion of labor!
phrases.notes: The hole still needs a peg to be put in, so the job is not finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה rule quoted in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that drilling any size hole makes one liable, as seen by שמואל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For שמואל, liability for a hole comes only from מכה בפטיש (completing the work). A drilled hole that is waiting for a peg is not complete.

steps.title: The case is one where an iron nail drilled the hole and was left in
steps.stepSummary: The משנה means someone drilled with an iron nail and left it in the hole, so the hole is already finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where he made the hole with an iron nail and left it inside, which counts as finishing the labor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case. The משנה is talking about a hole that is already finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a drilled hole is waiting for something to go into it. But if the nail that made the hole stays there for good, nothing else will be added. So even for שמואל, this counts as גמר מלאכה.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here? —
where he pierced it with an iron nail
and left it inside it,
which is the completion of labor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to be about an ordinary drilled hole that still needs a peg, which שמואל would not call finished.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a hole where the iron nail was left in place for good, so the job is done even for שמואל.
steps.whatToRemember: Even for שמואל, drilling makes one liable when the hole is already finished, for example when the drilling nail is left inside.

steps.title: What does 'this is the principle' come to include?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the words 'זה הכלל' from the משנה and asks what extra case they add.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'This is the principle.' What does 'this is the principle' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's general rule and asks what new case it is meant to cover. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in the משנה is that anyone who does a מלאכה that lasts on שבת is חייב. The גמרא assumes a general rule like this is not just a summary. It must add a case that the list did not already mention.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the principle (a general rule in the משנה)
To include what? (asking what extra case is added)

phrases.english: This is the principle.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: 'This is the principle' — to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case is added by the general phrase 'זה הכלל'.

steps.title: It includes carving a small measure in wood meant for a larger one
steps.stepSummary: 'זה הכלל' adds one who carved a קפיזא-sized hollow in wood meant to become a קב-sized vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: To include one who carved out a קפיזא in a block meant for a קב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the general rule adds a case where someone carved only part of a planned vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker planned to carve a full קב vessel but stopped after a smaller קפיזא hollow. Even though his plan is not finished, the small hollow can already be used as a measure, so the work lasts. Since it lasts, he is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: A small measure (a fraction of a קב)

phrases.english: To include one who carved a kefiza in a kav.
phrases.notes: The partly carved hollow is already usable as a smaller measure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The general rule adds carving a usable smaller measure inside wood meant for a bigger vessel.
steps.whatToRemember: Work that lasts and is useful on its own counts, even if the worker's bigger plan is not done.

steps.title: Why is striking the anvil with a hammer a labor?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view that striking a hammer on an anvil makes one liable, and asks what the person actually did.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: one who strikes an anvil with a sledgehammer, etc. What is he doing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and asks what מלאכה is done by striking the anvil. This sets up a series of answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hitting a hammer on an anvil does not seem to make or change anything. The גמרא wants to know why it counts as a מלאכה at all.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he doing? (what act did he perform)

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One who strikes with a sledgehammer on the anvil, etc.
What is he doing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the last line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What מלאכה is done by striking the anvil.

steps.title: רבה and רב יוסף: he is training his hand
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף explain that he is liable because he is training his hand for the craft.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both said: because he trains his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer is that striking the anvil is practice, and that practice is what counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this view, the act is not about changing any object. It improves the worker's skill, and that is treated as the liability.

phrases.english: It was Rabba and Rav Yosef who both said:
Because he trains his hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a first answer to the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Liability comes from training one's hand in the craft.

steps.title: בני רחבה: then watching and learning a craft would be liable too
steps.stepSummary: בני רחבה object that by this logic, someone who watched a craft on שבת and learned it would also be liable, which is absurd.
steps.simpleTranslation: בני רחבה found it difficult: if so, someone who saw a craft on שבת and learned it, would he also be liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the 'training the hand' answer by showing it leads to a strange result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If gaining skill alone made one liable, then just watching and learning would be a חילול שבת. Liability on שבת needs a real physical act of מלאכה, not just learning. So the training explanation cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (pointing out a strange result)

phrases.english: The sons of Rachava found it difficult:
But if so,
one who saw a craft on Shabbat and learned it,
would he also be liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה and רב יוסף's 'training the hand' explanation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reductio: if skill alone made one liable, learning by watching would also make one liable, which cannot be.

steps.title: אביי and רבא: the משכן metalworkers did this
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא explain that striking the anvil is a מלאכה because those who flattened metal plates for the משכן did it as part of their work.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי and רבא both said: because those who flattened the plates of the משכן did so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces the rejected answer with a new one tied to the work done in the משכן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All מלאכות of שבת are learned from the work of building the משכן. The metalworkers there would strike the anvil as part of their real work, according to the explanations given. So it is a real action from the משכן, not just practice, and that is why one is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who flatten or hammer thin
The Tabernacle, the source of the מלאכות of שבת

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the basic method for the מלאכות of שבת: an act counts if it matches a real action done in building the משכן.

phrases.english: Rather, it was Abaye and Rava who both said:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן מְרַדְּדֵי טַסֵּי מִשְׁכָּן עוֹשִׂין כֵּן.
phrases.english: Because those who flatten the plates of the Mishkan do so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 8 knocks down step 7, this gives a new answer to step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the rejected explanation with a new reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The liability was thought to come from training the hand.
steps.terutzMaskana: The liability comes from copying an action the משכן metalworkers really did.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports אביי and רבא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל giving exactly the reason of אביי and רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says, even one who strikes an anvil with a sledgehammer during work is liable, because those who flattened the plates of the משכן did so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up the answer of אביי and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states the משכן reason in רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's own words. It also adds 'בשעת מלאכה', during work, which shows the act is part of real work and not just practice.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא (a supporting source)

steps.whatToRemember: Striking the anvil makes one liable because the משכן metalworkers did it as part of their work, not because it trains one's hand.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even one who strikes with a sledgehammer on the anvil
during work — is liable,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן מְרַדְּדֵי טַסֵּי מִשְׁכָּן עוֹשִׂין כֵּן.
phrases.english: because those who flatten the plates of the Mishkan do so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 9.
steps.raayaObject: אביי and רבא's explanation, based on the משכן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבן שמעון בן גמליאל with the same reason.

steps.title: New משנה: plowing, weeding, and pruning any amount
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that plowing, weeding, clearing dry branches, or pruning even the smallest amount makes one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who plows any amount, and one who weeds, clears dry branches, or prunes any amount, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists field labors where even a tiny amount is enough for liability.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of these acts helps the land or the plants right away, so no minimum amount is needed. Plowing is a main מלאכה, and weeding and pruning help the land or trees grow, much like it.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
One who cuts off dry branches

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who plows any amount,
one who weeds, and one who clears dry branches, and one who prunes
any amount — is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the end of the previous discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Plowing, weeding, clearing dry branches, and pruning make one liable for any amount.

steps.title: Gathering wood or grass: the amount depends on the purpose
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that gathering wood or grass to improve the land makes one liable for any amount. Gathering wood for fuel needs enough to cook a light egg, and gathering grass for an animal needs a goat's mouthful.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who gathers wood: if to improve the land, any amount; if for fuel, enough to cook a light egg. One who gathers grass: if to improve the land, any amount; if for an animal, a goat's mouthful.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and shows that the same act can have a different minimum amount depending on why it was done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the goal is to improve the land, any amount helps, so any amount makes one liable. When the goal is to use what was gathered, he is liable only once he has a useful amount: enough wood to cook an easily cooked egg, or enough grass to fill a young goat's mouth.

keyTerms.meaning: An easily cooked egg (a small amount of cooking)

steps.confusionAlert: The act of gathering is the same in both cases. Only the purpose changes the minimum amount needed for liability.
steps.whatToRemember: If the goal is to improve the land, any amount makes one liable. If the goal is to use what was gathered, one is liable only for a useful amount.

phrases.english: One who gathers wood,
if to improve — any amount,

phrases.aramaic: אִם לְהֶיסֵּק — כְּדֵי לְבַשֵּׁל בֵּיצָה קַלָּה.
phrases.english: if for fuel — enough to cook a light egg.
One who gathers grass,
if to improve — any amount,
if for an animal — a goat's mouthful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with more field labors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The minimum amount for gathering wood or grass depends on purpose: any amount to improve the land, a useful amount (cooking a light egg, or a goat's mouthful) for use.

steps.title: What is plowing a tiny amount good for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what use a tiny amount of plowing has, since the משנה makes one liable for any amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: For what is it fit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by asking why plowing even a tiny bit counts as real work. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מלאכה on שבת usually needs to be big enough to be useful. The משנה said plowing 'any amount' makes one liable, so the גמרא wants to know what useful purpose such a tiny amount could have.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion of the משנה
For what is it fit? What use does it have?

phrases.english: GEMARA: For what is it fit?
phrases.notes: It refers to plowing 'any amount' from the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה's rulings to the גמרא's explanation of them.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What useful purpose a tiny amount of plowing has that would make it a real מלאכה.

steps.title: Enough to plant one pumpkin seed
steps.stepSummary: A tiny plowed spot can hold one pumpkin seed, which matches planting one dye-herb in the משכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is fit for a single pumpkin seed. The parallel in the משכן is that it is fit for one stalk of dye-herbs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even a tiny plowed spot is useful because a pumpkin seed can be planted there. It ties this to the משכן, where a single dye-plant could be grown in that much space.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All the מלאכות of שבת are modeled on the work done for the משכן. Since planting one dye-plant was meaningful work there, plowing a space big enough for one seed is also meaningful work.

keyTerms.meaning: The Tabernacle, the model for all מלאכות of שבת

phrases.english: It is fit for a pumpkin seed.
phrases.notes: A tiny spot is enough to plant a single seed.

phrases.english: Its parallel in the Tabernacle
phrases.notes: Every מלאכה needs a model in the משכן.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן רָאוּי לְקֶלַח אֶחָד שֶׁל סַמָּנִין.
phrases.english: is that it is fit for one stalk of dye-herbs.
phrases.notes: Plants were grown in the משכן work to make dyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Plowing a tiny amount is useful for planting one pumpkin seed, which parallels planting one dye-herb stalk for the משכן.

steps.title: Minimum amounts for cutting plants depend on the purpose
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives different minimum amounts for cutting endives or reeds, depending on why the person cut them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who weeds, clears dry branches, or prunes.' The Rabbis taught: One who pulls up endives or prunes reeds: if for eating, the amount is a dried fig; if for an animal, a goat's mouthful; if for fuel, enough to cook a light egg; if to improve the land, any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the words of the משנה and brings a ברייתא that sets the minimum amount for each purpose of cutting plants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount needed for liability depends on what the person wants the plants for. Food needs a fig's size, animal food needs a goat's mouthful, fuel needs enough to cook an egg, and improving the land counts at any amount. Purpose sets the measure.

keyTerms.meaning: Endives, wild plants that grow like weeds
Reeds or small shoots that are pruned
The size of a dried fig, the standard amount for food on שבת

phrases.english: One who weeds, and one who clears dry branches, and one who prunes.
phrases.notes: A quote of the words of the משנה being discussed.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
phrases.notes: Introduces a ברייתא.

phrases.english: One who pulls up endives or prunes reeds,
if for eating, the amount is a dried fig.
If for an animal, the amount is a goat's mouthful.

phrases.aramaic: אִם לְהֶיסֵּק — כְּדֵי לְבַשֵּׁל בֵּיצָה קַלָּה.
phrases.english: If for fuel, enough to cook a light egg.

phrases.aramaic: אִם לְיַיפּוֹת אֶת הַקַּרְקַע — כׇּל שֶׁהֵן.
phrases.english: If to improve the land, any amount.
phrases.notes: This last case is the one the גמרא questions next.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה and adds a ברייתא that explains it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The minimum amount for liability when cutting plants depends on the purpose: food is a fig's size, animal food is a goat's mouthful, fuel is enough to cook an egg, and improving the land is any amount.

steps.title: Doesn't every cut improve the land?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: pulling up any plant improves the land, so why do the other purposes need larger amounts?
steps.simpleTranslation: Aren't all of these also improving the land?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא's split between purposes. Whatever the person's reason, pulling up plants clears the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If improving the land makes one liable for any amount, then the person who cuts for food or fuel has also improved the land. So he should be liable for any amount too. That would make the larger amounts for food, animals, and fuel meaningless.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? Opens a question of surprise
To improve or beautify the land

phrases.english: Is that to say that all of them
phrases.notes: Refers to all the purposes listed in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: are not improving the land?
phrases.notes: Every pulled plant clears the ground.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כּוּלְּהוּ לָא לְיַפּוֹת אֶת הַקַּרְקַע נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא quoted in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's separate measures for food, animal, and fuel.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every act of uprooting also improves the land, so every case should carry liability for any amount, which wipes out the larger measures.

steps.title: The case is a swamp
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף answer that the ברייתא is about a swamp, where pulling plants does not improve the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both said: They taught this about a swamp.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה and רב יוסף answer the challenge. The ברייתא is talking about swampland, where clearing plants does nothing for the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a swamp the land is not used for farming, so cutting plants there does not improve it. That is why the purpose of the cutting, food, animal, or fuel, sets the amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Swamp or marsh, land not used for farming

phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef both said:
They taught this about a swamp.
phrases.notes: No farming improvement happens there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific location
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is about ordinary farmland, where every cut improves the land.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a swamp, where cutting gives no benefit to the land.

steps.title: אביי: The person did not intend to improve the land
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that even in a normal field, the case is one where the person did not mean to improve the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: You can even say it is a field that is not a swamp, in a case where he did not intend to improve the land.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a different answer. The ברייתא can be about a regular field if the person was not trying to improve the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי moves the answer from where the act happened to what the person was thinking. If the cutter only wanted food or fuel, the land improvement is an unintended side effect, so the amount follows his real purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: An act whose result was not intended

phrases.english: Abaye said:
You can even say it is a field that is not a swamp,
in a case where he does not intend to improve the land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the challenge of step 16, different from רבה and רב יוסף.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case by the person's intention
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a swamp can explain the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a regular field works, if the person had no intention to improve the land.

steps.title: But a result that is certain counts anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי from his own rule: רבי שמעון agrees one is liable when the result is unavoidable (פסיק רישיה).
steps.simpleTranslation: But אביי and רבא both said: רבי שמעון agrees in the case of 'cut off its head and will it not die?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי using a rule that אביי himself said with רבא. Lack of intention does not help when the result is certain to happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון normally excuses a result the person did not intend. But he agrees that if the result is unavoidable, like cutting off a head and expecting the animal to live, the person is liable. Pulling up plants surely improves the land, so not intending it should not help.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that... Opens a challenge
Cut off its head and will it not die? A result that is certain to happen

steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון usually excuses an act done without intention. פסיק רישיה is the exception: if the result is certain, saying 'I didn't mean it' does not help.

phrases.english: But Abaye and Rava both said:
Rabbi Shimon agrees
phrases.notes: Even though he usually excuses a result that was not intended.

phrases.english: in the case of 'cut off its head and will it not die?'
phrases.notes: When the result is certain, intention does not matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that lack of intention removes the 'improving the land' liability.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Improving the land is a certain result of uprooting, and אביי himself holds that a certain result counts even without intention.

steps.title: It is someone else's field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that אביי was speaking about someone working in another person's field, where he gets no benefit from the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed only where he does it in his friend's land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves אביי's answer by limiting it to a case where the field belongs to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The improvement still happens, but the person does not care about it because it is not his land. So the improvement is not treated as his goal, and only his real purpose, like food or fuel, sets the amount.

keyTerms.meaning: It was only needed for this case
His friend's land, someone else's field

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's separate measures fit a case where improving the land is not the person's real goal: a swamp (רבה and רב יוסף), or someone else's field where he has no interest in the improvement (אביי).

phrases.english: It was only needed
phrases.notes: Limits אביי's case.

phrases.english: where he does it in his friend's land.
phrases.notes: He gets no benefit from the improvement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 and keeps אביי's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי's case is any field, so the certain improvement should make the person liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: אביי's case is someone else's field, where the improvement is of no interest to the person.

steps.title: Writing two letters makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that writing two letters on שבת makes one liable, in any hand, letters, inks, or language.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who writes two letters, whether with his right hand or his left, whether the same letter or two different letters, whether in two inks, in any language, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about the מלאכה of writing. Two letters are enough for liability, and many details do not change that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The minimum for writing is two letters. Using either hand, repeating the same letter, mixing two inks, or writing in any language all still count.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who writes two letters,
whether with his right hand or his left,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִשֵּׁם אֶחָד בֵּין מִשְּׁנֵי שֵׁמוֹת
phrases.english: whether the same letter twice or two different letters,
whether in two different inks,
in any language, is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new מלאכה, writing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing two letters on שבת makes one liable, whatever the hand, letters, inks, or language.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: Two letters count because they are a mark
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי explains that two letters count because of marking, like the marks on the boards of the משכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said: They made one liable for two letters only because of marking, since that is how they wrote on the boards of the Tabernacle to know which board was the partner of which.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי explains where the two-letter rule comes from. In the משכן, marks were written on the boards to match each board with its neighbor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוסי, the source of liability is marking, not writing words with meaning. Two signs were enough in the משכן to pair the boards, so two letters are enough on שבת.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said:
They made one liable for two letters
only because of marking,
since that is how they wrote on the boards of the Tabernacle
to know which board was its partner.
phrases.notes: So the boards could be put back in the same order each time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a reason for the משנה's two-letter rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two letters make one liable because of marking, based on the marks on the boards of the משכן.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: A short name inside a longer name
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה shows that two letters can form a complete short name that is also the start of a longer name.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: We find a short name within a long name: 'שם' from שמעון and from שמואל, 'נח' from נחור, 'דן' from דניאל, 'גד' from גדיאל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a different reason for the two-letter rule. Two letters can already be a full name, even when the writer planned a longer one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who starts writing שמעון and stops after two letters has written שם, a real word. So two letters count as meaningful writing even if the longer word was never finished.

keyTerms.meaning: A short name taken from a long name

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה makes one liable for two letters. רבי יוסי says this is because of marking, as in the משכן. רבי יהודה says it is because two letters can already form a complete short name.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
We find a short name within a long name:
'Shem' from Shimon and from Shmuel,
'Noach' from Nachor, 'Dan' from Daniel,
'Gad' from Gaddiel.
phrases.notes: In each case the first two letters of the long name make a complete short name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different reason from רבי יוסי for the two-letter rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two letters make one liable because they can form a complete short name, even when the writer meant to write a longer one.

steps.title: Why is writing with the left hand liable?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה makes someone liable for writing with the left hand, since people do not normally write that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense to be liable for writing with the right hand, because that is how people write. But why be liable for the left hand? People do not write that way!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by challenging one detail. The משנה said you are liable for writing 'with either hand.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מלאכה on שבת usually counts only when it is done the normal way (דרך כתיבה). Most people write with the right hand. So writing with the left hand seems unusual, and an unusual action should not make someone liable.

phrases.english: Gemara:
Granted, for writing with the right hand let him be liable,
because that is the normal way of writing.
But for writing with the left hand, why is he liable?
That is not the normal way of writing!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא אַיָּמִין לִיחַיַּיב מִשּׁוּם דְּדֶרֶךְ כְּתִיבָה בְּכָךְ, אֶלָּא אַשְּׂמֹאל אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה from Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that writing with either hand makes one liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A מלאכה only counts when done the normal way. Left-handed writing is not normal, so it should not count.

steps.title: The משנה is about a left-handed person
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה answers that the משנה is talking about a left-handed person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: They taught this about a left-handed person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the question. For a left-handed person, writing with the left hand is normal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer changes the case. The משנה is not talking about an ordinary person who uses his weaker hand. It is talking about someone whose main hand is the left, so for him that is the normal way to write.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
They taught it about a left-handed person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: בְּאִטֵּר יָד שָׁנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 24.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about an ordinary right-handed person writing with the left hand.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a left-handed person, for whom the left hand is normal.

steps.title: Then the right hand should not count for him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבי ירמיה's answer: for a left-handed person, the right hand should be the unusual one, but the משנה says either hand makes him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then his left hand should count like everyone else's right hand. He should be liable for the left hand and not liable for the right hand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי ירמיה's answer. The משנה said 'either hand,' and a left-handed person still has an unusual hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a left-handed person, the hands are simply reversed. His left is his 'normal' hand and his right is his 'unusual' hand. So the משנה should say he is liable only for his left hand. That does not fit the words 'either hand.'

phrases.english: But let his left hand be treated
like everyone else's right hand,
so for the left hand let him be liable,
and for the right hand let him not be liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתֶהֱוֵי שְׂמֹאל דִּידֵיהּ כְּיָמִין דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's answer that the משנה is about a left-handed person
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A left-handed person has the hands reversed. His right hand would then be unusual, but the משנה says either hand makes him liable.

steps.title: The משנה is about someone who uses both hands equally
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the משנה is talking about an ambidextrous person, who writes normally with both hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: It is talking about someone who controls both hands equally.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new answer that replaces רבי ירמיה's answer. For an ambidextrous person, both hands write normally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא ('rather') shows that the earlier answer is dropped. Since this person writes equally well with each hand, neither hand is unusual for him. That is why the משנה can say 'either hand.'
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's 'either hand' refers to an ambidextrous person, for whom both hands are a normal way of writing.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
It refers to one who controls both his hands equally.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: בְּשׁוֹלֵט בִּשְׁתֵּי יָדָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of Step 25 with a new case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New אוקימתא replacing the earlier one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about a left-handed person.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about an ambidextrous person, so both hands count as normal writing.

steps.title: Another answer: the משנה follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: רב יעקב says the משנה follows רבי יוסי, who holds that two letters make one liable because they work as marking, so neat writing is not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יעקב, the son of the daughter of יעקב, said: Whose view is this? It is רבי יוסי, who said that two letters make one liable only because of marking.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יעקב gives a different way to explain why the left hand counts. He says the משנה follows רבי יוסי from Step 22.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוסי, the reason for liability is making a mark (רושם), like the marks on the boards of the משכן. A mark does not need to be written the usual way or neatly. So even left-handed writing by an ordinary person counts.

phrases.aramaic: רַב יַעֲקֹב בְּרֵהּ דְּבַת יַעֲקֹב אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Ya'akov, son of the daughter of Ya'akov, said:
Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Yosei's,
who said: they made one liable for two letters
only because of marking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the question of Step 24, different from אביי's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה follows רבי יוסי. Since liability comes from marking, writing with the left hand also counts.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a specific תנא (רבי יוסי)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Liability for writing requires the normal manner of writing, so an ordinary person writing with his left hand should be exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה follows רבי יוסי, for whom liability comes from making a mark (רושם), so even unusual left-handed writing counts.

steps.title: But רבי יוסי is named only in the later part
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the משנה names רבי יוסי only in its later clause, which suggests the first clause is not his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the later part of the משנה is רבי יוסי, the first part is not רבי יוסי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יעקב. If רבי יוסי's name appears only in the later part of the משנה, it seems the earlier part belongs to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a משנה names a תנא partway through, it usually means the earlier part was not his opinion. The 'either hand' rule is in the first part (רישא). So it would not be רבי יוסי's view, and רב יעקב's answer seems to fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: The later part of a משנה
The first part of a משנה

phrases.english: But from the fact that the later clause is Rabbi Yosei,
the first clause is not Rabbi Yosei!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מִדְּסֵיפָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הִיא, רֵישָׁא לָאו רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יעקב's claim from Step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יעקב's claim that the first part of the משנה follows רבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Naming רבי יוסי only in the later part suggests the first part is an anonymous view that differs from his.

steps.title: The whole משנה is רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the entire משנה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The whole משנה is רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יעקב. It says that all of the משנה, start to end, follows רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming רבי יוסי in the later part does not have to mean the first part disagrees with him. The משנה can state his rule first and then give his reasoning with his name attached. So the 'either hand' rule fits his view about marking.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers to the left-hand question: אביי says the משנה is about an ambidextrous person, and רב יעקב says it follows רבי יוסי's view that writing counts as marking.

phrases.english: The entire mishna is Rabbi Yosei.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the inference from the name being placed later
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רבי יוסי is named only in the later part, the first part is someone else's view.
steps.terutzMaskana: The whole משנה is רבי יוסי. His name in the later part does not split the משנה into two views.

steps.title: Does רבי יהודה require two different letters?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's 'we found' and asks whether he makes someone liable only for two different letters, and not for the same letter written twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: 'We found.' Does this mean that for רבי יהודה, only two letters that are two different letters make one liable, but two letters that are the same letter do not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to רבי יהודה's statement in the משנה (Step 23). It asks what his example implies, and this sets up a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's example, like שם from שמעון, uses two different letters. That could imply he does not count the same letter written twice. The גמרא is about to test whether that is really his view.

keyTerms.meaning: One type of letter (the same letter repeated)

steps.confusionAlert: Here שם does not mean 'name.' It means a 'type' of letter. 'Two שמות' means two different letters, and 'one שם' means the same letter written twice.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said: We found.
Is it then that Rabbi Yehuda
holds that two letters that are two different letters
are what make one liable,

phrases.aramaic: שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת וְהֵן שֵׁם אֶחָד — לָא מְחַיֵּיב?
phrases.english: but two letters that are the same letter do not make one liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת וְהֵן שְׁנֵי שֵׁמוֹת הוּא דִּמְחַיֵּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic: what רבי יהודה's statement in Step 23 implies.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי יהודה requires the two letters to be different letters for liability.

steps.title: A ברייתא: liable even without finishing the whole job
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to quote a ברייתא that learns from 'מאחת' that one is liable even for part of a job, like part of a name, garment, or sieve.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא taught: 'And he did one.' You might think he is not liable until he writes the whole name, weaves the whole garment, or makes the whole sieve. So the verse says: 'from one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the idea from Step 31. The ברייתא continues in Step 33 and on the next amud, where it will show רבי יהודה's own view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first asks whether one is liable only for finishing a complete job. The verse says 'from one' (מאחת), which means even part of a job counts. The rest of this ברייתא, continuing in Step 33 and on the next amud, will be used to test what רבי יהודה holds about letters that are the same.

keyTerms.meaning: From one (even part of a job)

phrases.english: But was it not taught: 'And he did' one?
One might think: not until he writes the entire name,
and not until he weaves the entire garment,
and not until he makes the entire sieve.
Therefore the verse says: 'from one.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the challenge to the idea raised in Step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רבי יהודה does not count the same letter written twice
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא about 'מאחת' (continuing later) will show a different view in רבי יהודה's name.

steps.title: The ברייתא worries that even one letter, one thread, or one sieve-eye might be enough
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if 'מאחת' means part of a job is enough, maybe even the tiniest piece makes one liable, like a single letter, a single thread, or a single eye of a sieve.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we learn from 'מאחת' that part of a job is enough, I might have thought a person is liable even if he wrote only one letter, wove only one thread, or made only one eye in a sieve.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still quoting the ברייתא it began in Step 32. Here the ברייתא raises a possible but mistaken reading, which sets up the limit it will give next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 showed that 'מאחת' teaches that a person can be liable for part of a job. Now the ברייתא tests how far that idea goes: could even the smallest possible piece count? The word יכול tells us this is a 'one might think' idea that the ברייתא will soon reject. That rejection is what the גמרא needs for its challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One might think.' It introduces a possible reading that will be rejected.
One 'eye' (opening) in a sieve, made by weaving one reed across the frame

steps.confusionAlert: This is NOT the ברייתא's final ruling. 'יכול' introduces a wrong idea that the ברייתא is about to reject. Do not learn from this line that one letter makes a person liable.

phrases.english: If [we learn only] from "from one,"
phrases.notes: Refers back to the word the ברייתא used in Step 32.

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא אוֹת אַחַת,
phrases.english: one might think [he is liable] even if he wrote only one letter,
or wove only one thread,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עָשָׂה אֶלָּא בַּיִת אֶחָד בַּנָּפָה,
phrases.english: or made only one eye in a sieve,
phrases.notes: A sieve is woven from reeds. One 'eye' is the smallest woven unit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי ״מֵאַחַת״, יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא אוֹת אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quotation begun in Step 32. It adds the ברייתא's 'one might think' step before the ברייתא sets its limit.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question in Step 31 about whether רבי יהודה makes someone liable only for two different letters.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The quote is still being built. The ברייתא's coming limit on the minimum amount, and the examples it uses, will be brought to bear on רבי יהודה's view.
steps.whyThisMatters: This 'one might think' sets up the ברייתא's rule for the smallest piece of a job that still counts. That rule is the key to the question about רבי יהודה.
